title: How Police Body Cameras Work
summary: Josh and Chuck explore police body-worn cameras: the 2012 Rialto, California pilot study and its results (less force, fewer complaints, self-awareness and spillover effects), how the technology works (chest mount, wide-angle lens, timestamps, GPS, buffering pre-record), the 2014 Eric Garner and Michael Brown cases that spurred national attention and a Department of Justice grant program, debates about whether cameras build or erode trust, camera policies on when to record, costs, data storage and retention and cloud systems (including Taser's system), access and disclosure laws, the Tyler Stewart shooting footage in Arizona, the Utah nurse arrest footage, video manipulation and facial recognition concerns, and peer-reviewed study limits. The episode closes with listener mail from a five-year-old fan in Scotland named Noah.
topics: Department of Justice body camera grants
disclosure and FOIA of police video

segments.title: Opening banter
segments.summary: Josh and Chuck introduce the episode on body cameras and joke about the show's recent law enforcement episodes.

segments.title: Rialto pilot study
segments.summary: The 2012 Rialto, California pilot gave half the police force body cameras; officers using them used force less and complaints dropped about nine percent. Researchers described self-awareness and spillover effects.

segments.title: Ferguson, Eric Garner and the national push
segments.summary: Eric Garner's 2014 death, captured on cell phone video, and Michael Brown's shooting by Darren Wilson sparked national debate. Rialto's results spurred cities to adopt cameras and the Department of Justice offered forty-three million dollars in grants.
topics: Department of Justice body camera grants

segments.title: Do cameras solve distrust?
segments.summary: The hosts debate whether cameras fix the trust problem or underscore mutual distrust, and whether they risk lulling people into complacency. They note cameras are a tool, not a magic pill.

segments.title: How the cameras work and recording policies
segments.summary: Cameras are typically chest-mounted and have timestamps, badge numbers, GPS, still photos, and streaming. Recording policies vary by department; one survey found only three percent of officers recorded seven or more hours per day. Facial recognition and a pre-record buffer are described.

segments.title: Costs, data storage and access
segments.summary: Costs range from about four to nine dollars per camera. Oakland's six hundred cameras generate about seven terabytes monthly. Retention periods vary by city, and Taser offers a cloud system that logs access. Disclosure laws let media request footage.

segments.title: Footage release, privacy and the Tyler Stewart shooting
segments.summary: Officer Tyler Stewart's body camera recorded his killing by Robert Smith in Arizona, raising questions about release of footage and family privacy. The hosts discuss the competing privacy interests of citizens and officers.

segments.title: Limits of single-angle video and new risks
segments.summary: A single body camera gives a biased view; the Utah nurse arrest showed a second officer's camera changed the picture. Video editing, multiple viewpoints, civilian cameras from Wolf Com, and private facial recognition in stores are discussed, plus limited peer-reviewed research.

segments.title: Listener mail from Noah
segments.summary: A five-year-old listener in Scotland, Noah, writes in asking for an episode on bridges, and his mother notes her three-year-old daughter does not like the show.

segments.title: Sign-off
segments.summary: Hosts give contact information and sign off.
